Article Title: New York spent 8 years planting one million trees. Now the city is aiming for 30% tree cover by 2040 to transform its fight against rising heat
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

How New York planted one million trees to reshape its urban landscape

Why planting trees does more than add green spaces

How tree cover helps reduce heat in vulnerable communities

The growing economic and environmental value of city trees

How New York is growing its tree canopy beyond one million trees

For decades, New York has been associated with skyscrapers, traffic and tightly packed neighbourhoods rather than large-scale environmental restoration. Yet across the city's streets, parks and residential areas, an enormous change has been taking place almost unnoticed. Trees planted years ago are now reaching maturity, casting wider shade over pavements, cooling busy roads and gradually altering the character of many communities. As hotter summers become more common, the long-term value of those earlier planting efforts is becoming easier to measure.New York's attention has now shifted from reaching a numerical milestone to expanding tree cover across the city in a more balanced way. As reported by NYC Mayor's Office of Climate & Environmental Justice, officials have set a goal of increasing overall canopy coverage to roughly 30% by 2040, while continuing to prioritise neighbourhoods that experience the greatest exposure to extreme heat.In 2007, New York City launched MillionTreesNYC with a target that sounded unusually large even by the city's standards: planting one million trees across the five boroughs.The work extended well beyond parks. New trees appeared beside streets, inside school grounds, around public housing developments, near hospitals and places of worship, and on many pieces of public land that previously had little vegetation.The campaign depended on far more than municipal workers. Community groups, volunteers and environmental organisations all became part of the effort, with the New York Restoration Project serving as one of the leading partners. Thousands of residents also took part by helping with planting events across their neighbourhoods. Reportedly, the millionth tree was planted in 2015, reaching the goal ahead of the original schedule.Planting trees was never simply about making neighbourhoods look greener. City planners viewed the expanding urban forest as infrastructure capable of providing practical environmental benefits for decades after each sapling entered the ground.As the trees matured, they began changing local conditions in small but measurable ways. Streets with larger canopies receive less direct sunlight, reducing the amount of heat absorbed by asphalt and concrete. At the same time, trees release moisture through their leaves, which helps cool the surrounding air naturally during warm weather.Heat does not affect every part of New York equally. Areas with fewer trees and large expanses of pavement often experience noticeably higher temperatures than neighbourhoods with greater vegetation.Many of these hotter districts have historically had lower tree coverage, leaving residents with fewer shaded public spaces during prolonged heatwaves. That has influenced more recent planning decisions, with city authorities directing new planting programmes towards communities identified as being especially vulnerable to rising temperatures.The approach reflects a wider understanding that urban forestry is connected to public health as much as environmental policy. Access to shade, lower outdoor temperatures and cleaner air can all contribute to reducing some of the pressures associated with extreme summer heat.The value of an urban forest increases as trees age. Mature canopies intercept rainfall before it reaches drains, helping reduce stormwater runoff during heavy downpours. Trees also capture airborne pollutants and absorb carbon dioxide while producing oxygen.These environmental services have economic value as well. According to the press release in New York City Comptroller Mark Levine dated 23 April 2026, city estimates suggest New York's urban forest now generates around $120 million in annual environmental and financial benefits through cleaner air, lower energy demand, improved stormwater management and related ecosystem services.Unlike many infrastructure projects that begin to deteriorate soon after construction, healthy trees often become more effective as they mature, provided they receive regular care and protection.Completing the original planting target did not mark the end of the programme. Maintaining existing trees has become just as important as adding new ones. Young trees require watering, pruning and monitoring during their early years, while older specimens need continued management to remain healthy and safe in an increasingly challenging climate.Volunteer stewardship programmes continue to encourage residents to care for street trees, remove litter from planting areas and support local conservation projects. Public mapping tools also allow people to identify individual street trees and record maintenance activities, creating greater community involvement in managing the city's expanding canopy.
Article Summary: In 2007, New York City launched MillionTreesNYC with a target that sounded unusually large even by the city's standards: planting one million trees. The millionth tree was planted in 2015, reaching the goal ahead of the original schedule. Officials have set a goal of increasing overall canopy coverage to roughly 30% by 2040.

Article Title: 'Could result in injuries': FAA flags incorrectly installed seats on several Boeing 737 Max jets
Article Text:
FAA stated the possibility of injuries to passengers during emergency landings

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has proposed mandatory inspections of passenger seats on 453 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft registered in the United States after reports that some seat assemblies may have been installed incorrectly.The FAA said improperly installed seat assemblies could disengage from the seat tracks during turbulence or an emergency landing, potentially injuring passengers and crew or blocking the aisle and delaying evacuation, reported Reuters. "This condition, if not addressed, could result in injury ‌to passengers and crew during an emergency landing or could block the aisle, which could slow evacuation," it added.The proposed airworthiness directive, issued on Monday, follows a report that some passenger seat assemblies were not correctly secured in the seat tracks. The agency said each aircraft could have up to 69 track-mounted passenger seat assemblies, with inspections and corrective work expected to take about one hour per seat assembly without requiring replacement parts.A Boeing spokesrperson said in an email that, "We support the FAA making that guidance mandatory."The directive applies only to US-registered aircraft, although aviation regulators in other countries often adopt similar FAA safety measures when applicable. The FAA has not yet specified a deadline for airlines to complete the inspections.The move comes as Boeing continues efforts to improve manufacturing quality under CEO Kelly Ortberg following heightened regulatory scrutiny after a door plug panel blew out of an Alaska Airlines 737 MAX during flight in early 2024.A Boeing spokesperson said the company had already issued guidance to airlines on the issue in December 2025 and supports the FAA's decision to make those recommendations mandatory.
Article Summary: FAA has proposed mandatory inspections of passenger seats on 453 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft registered in the United States. FAA said improperly installed seat assemblies could disengage from the seat tracks during turbulence or an emergency landing. Move comes as Boeing continues efforts to improve manufacturing quality under CEO Kelly Ortberg.

Article Title: French wildfire created a monster cloud, unleashing lightning that ignited more fires
Article Text:
Monster cloud created by the wildfires

An electrified black thundercloud

Lightning and more destruction follow

In Europe, pyroCbs have been rare

PARIS: A wildfire in southwest France grew so powerful that its smoke column became a thunderstorm, generating lightning that struck the ground and ignited new fires beyond the original blaze, French officials said.Put another way, that means the inferno was no longer simply being propelled by the weather. It was making its own. The thundercloud also produced violent, erratic winds capable of driving the flames in new directions.The phenomenon, called a pyrocumulonimbus, or pyroCb, is rare in Europe and more commonly documented in North America and Australia, where it occurs only over some of the most extreme fires. France's national firefighters federation said it had never before recorded one in the country.The blaze erupted near Saumos on July 22 and has since burned more than 420 square kilometers (162 square miles) of forests and scrubland, damaged or destroyed more than 240 homes and forced 220,000 people to evacuate in Gironde.At about 6:20 p.m. Friday, two days after the fire began, the departmental fire and rescue service said it had generated a pyrocumulonimbus. The cloud weakened overnight as humidity rose, then formed again several times.Repeatedly, heat and smoke have surged upward into a vast black thundercloud, electrified and lit from within."Imagine a campfire so large and hot that the smoke rising off it turns into a storm-like cloud," said Theodore M. Giannaros, a fire meteorologist at the National Observatory of Athens."That is a pyroCb - a storm cloud born from the intense heat that a wildfire produces."It takes more than a big fire.There is no set temperature at which one forms, Giannaros said; what is needed is the kind of atmosphere that breeds dry thunderstorms - very hot, very dry air near the ground, with cooler and moister air above it.Hot air loaded with smoke and moisture then rises rapidly from the flames. As it climbs and cools, water vapor condenses around particles of ash.Above the freezing level, droplets become ice crystals whose collisions separate electrical charges, as in an ordinary thunderstorm.Beneath this storm lies a landscape already primed to burn. The cloud then amplifies the disaster that created it.Rising air pulls powerful winds toward the fire, while downdrafts punch gusts back to the surface.Those shifts can turn the flames, divide them into several fronts or send them racing in a new direction."It's a feedback loop, not a one-way effect," Giannaros said. "Once it forms, the cloud becomes its own weather system, sitting on top of the fire and making it harder to predict."The systems can also spin up whirling columns of flame - usually a fire whirl, which Giannaros describes as a dust devil made of fire and heat instead of dust.True tornadoes are rarer, though one struck Redding, California, during the 2018 Carr Fire with winds equivalent to an EF-3, killing a fire inspector.For firefighters, escape routes can close without warning as fresh outbreaks appear beyond their crews and equipment.Direct attack may become impossible, forcing crews to retreat and defend communities.The danger, Giannaros said, is fire moving faster than evacuations can be organized.Until now, pyroCbs have been essentially an Australian and North American phenomenon. Canada alone produced a record 142 of them in 2023.Portugal recorded one during its deadly 2017 fire season. France has now joined the list.The continent is heating faster than any other on Earth - at roughly twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service and the World Meteorological Organization - with heat waves growing more frequent and severe and drought spreading across the south, curing forests into fuel.Hotter and drier conditions give extreme fires more opportunity to form them, Giannaros said, but scientists still lack enough long-term data to establish a trend.The European research project ROSETTA aims to close that gap.The most common misunderstanding, he said, is that the cloud is merely a side effect. As long as it hangs above the flames, it is helping decide where the fire goes next.
Article Summary: A wildfire in southwest France grew so powerful that its smoke column became a thunderstorm. The phenomenon, called a pyrocumulonimbus, or pyroCb, is rare in Europe. It is more commonly documented in North America and Australia.

Article Title: Keigo Higashino, author of 'The Devotion of Suspect X', dies at 68
Article Text:
File photo: Keigo Higashino

Japanese mystery fiction author Keigo Higashino has died aged 68, his publisher said on Monday, triggering an outpouring of grief among fans across Asia.Since his 1985 debut, Higashino wrote more than 100 books, with his works translated and published in over 40 countries and territories, and widely adapted for film and television. "Author Keigo Higashino passed away due to colon cancer in the early morning of July 23. He was 68," publisher Kodansha said in a statement.A statement posted on Higashino's X account said that the author's "published works, from his debut novel 'After School', released in Sept 1985, to his latest book 'Eternal Memory', scheduled for release on Aug 5, 2026, total 106 books".Known for his versatility, the award-winning novelist had worked as an engineer before switching to writing full-time. His books merge science and detective fiction alongside acute observations on human nature and heartwarming tearjerkers, according to major bookstore chain Maruzen Junkudo.Higashino, whose books include "The Devotion of Suspect X" and "Malice", enjoyed a loyal following around Asia, including in China where thousands of people took to social media to mourn the writer. His "The Keeper of the Camphor Tree" was turned into an animated film, and the "Galileo" series of detective novels became a live-action TV series.According to Higashino's publisher, his books have topped 100 million copies in domestic circulation.Former novelist turned ultraconservative politician Naoki Hyakuta described Higashino on X as a "truly talented writer". "He understood what a story is, and what excellent writing is," he wrote.In China, Higashino's passing became one of the top trending topics on social media platform Weibo. Despite the volatile diplomatic ties between Beijing and Tokyo, his works have long been popular among readers in China. "The Miracles of the Namiya General Store" sold more than 10 million copies within its first four years in the mainland Chinese market, according to news portal ifeng.com.He was also popular in South Korea. "I've read so many of Keigo Higashino's books, and this feels so surreal. There are still so many of his books I haven't gotten around to reading yet," said a Threads user in Korea. "Higashino had always been there ever since I was a kid, and thanks to him, I was able to become a mystery novelist in South Korea," author Park Ha-ru said.(BY AFP)
Article Summary: Japanese mystery fiction author Keigo Higashino has died aged 68. His death triggered an outpouring of grief among fans across Asia. The award-winning novelist had worked as an engineer before switching to writing full-time. His books have topped 100 million copies in domestic circulation.

Article Title: Study shows world spoke tens of thousands more languages in antiquity than today
Article Text:
People currently use roughly 7,500 languages, finds study

WASHINGTON: Globally, people currently use roughly 7,500 languages, with English, Mandarin Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, Arabic and French the most common, counting native and non-native speakers. That is a lot of languages. But it is a far cry from the peak number historically.Researchers used mathematical modelling and insights from anthropology, linguistics and demography to estimate the number of languages used globally dating back about 12,000 years to around the end of the last Ice Age, covering a chapter in time called the Holocene epoch. They identified a period spanning the first millennium BC and first millennium AD when humankind may have spoken tens of thousands of different languages.The researchers also charted a major decline since this linguistic "golden age," due to language replacement driven by factors such as the expansion of large empires in antiquity and European colonialism in the past several centuries. "Languages are meaningful to their communities. They carry knowledge, associations and memories," said Claire Bowern, a professor of linguistics and anthropology at Yale University in Connecticut, and a leader of the study published in the journal Science.Many language families arose and evolved, with written language eventually emerging, first in Mesopotamia - Sumerian written in cuneiform script - during the fourth millennium BC, and separately in places like Egypt, China and Mesoamerica. The researchers estimated that the number topped out in a range from 30,000 to potentially more than 75,000 different languages used worldwide at any one time.The researchers used some ingenuity in reaching their estimates. "There's no direct evidence for language numbers until very recently. We cannot rely on the extremely patchy records from antiquity. But because we know a lot about the relationships between languages and societies, we can use a couple of assumptions to make a simulation model of language diversification through time," Bowern said.The researchers used data spanning 171 extant hunter-gatherer societies in Africa, South America and Southeast Asia to assess the size of ethno-linguistic groups near the beginning of the Holocene. They applied that to estimates of the human population at the time. People were dispersed in small bands around the world, living as nomadic hunter-gatherers. The researchers estimated that these scattered populations some 12,000 years ago spoke perhaps 4,500 to 6,200 languages.Bowern described some ways languages disappear. "The people who speak that language are killed or the people who speak that language shift or are forced to shift to another language," Bowern said. About half of languages used today are deemed endangered. Bowern said that "90% of the world's population speaks 10% of the world's languages, so there are many languages with small numbers of speakers."(BY REUTERS)
Article Summary: English, Mandarin Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, Arabic and French the most common. Researchers used mathematical modelling and insights from anthropology, linguistics and demography to estimate the number of languages used globally. They identified a period spanning the first millennium BC and first millennium AD when humankind may have spoken tens of thousands of languages.

Article Title: France, Spain race against time as wildfires force 320,000 evacuations
Article Text:
Europe battles raging wildfires

Firefighters across France and Spain are battling to contain massive wildfires as soaring temperatures and dry conditions fuel the blazes, with authorities warning that another heatwave expected later this week could hamper firefighting efforts and increase the risk of further spread.European Union officials have warned that wildfires could continue burning until early November, with the prolonged fire season threatening to make this one of the worst years on record for the total area of land destroyed by wildfires.Authorities have evacuated around 220,000 people, including residents and holidaymakers, across France as wildfires continue to spread. In neighbouring Spain, nearly 100,000 people have been ordered to evacuate or remain sheltered as firefighters battle multiple fast-moving blazes, as cited by Reuters.Spain's interior minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska described Monday and Tuesday as "absolutely crucial days" in the fight against the wildfires, warning that temperatures are expected to climb again from Wednesday.Meanwhile, a blaze in the hilly province of Ávila, west of Madrid, has become the largest wildfire on record in Spain after scorching 50,000 hectares (125,000 acres).Authorities are also battling two separate fires north-west of the capital, with the total area burned around Madrid reaching about 70,000 hectares.France is also in a race against time to contain the wildfires before another intense heatwave sets in later this week, according to fire service spokesperson Eric Brocardi, as cited by The Guardian.Weather forecasters have warned that temperatures could climb to as high as 40°C (104°F) in parts of the country from Tuesday, raising fears that the extreme heat will further fuel the blazes and complicate firefighting efforts.“The coming weeks will be tough and we have to hold out," said French president Emmanuel Macron while on a visit to Bordeaux.The looming heatwave is expected to further hinder efforts to contain the wildfire in Gironde, in south-western France.Interior minister Laurent Nuñez described the blaze as "extremely intense and unpredictable", warning that it is generating its own winds and advancing erratically towards the Bordeaux metropolitan area.A European Commission official said this year's wildfire season began in April and is expected to continue until early November, with authorities warning of heightened wildfire risks in France, Spain and Greece as temperatures rise again from the middle of the week.After France and Spain activated the European Union's emergency assistance mechanism, the European Commission coordinated the deployment of seven firefighting aircraft and four helicopters to France, along with six aircraft and three forest firefighting teams to Spain.EU officials have also been dispatched to the Bordeaux region to support local authorities in managing the crisis.
Article Summary: Authorities have evacuated around 220,000 people, including residents and holidaymakers, across France as wildfires continue to spread. A blaze in the hilly province of Ávila, west of Madrid, has become the largest wildfire on record in Spain. Weather forecasters have warned that temperatures could climb to as high as 40°C (104°F) in parts of the country from Tuesday, raising fears that the extreme heat will further fuel the blazes.

Article Title: Netanyahu, Zelenskyy in Washington for Graham's funeral as Trump hosts high-stakes war talks
Article Text: US president Donald Trump is set to host Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the White House on Tuesday (local time) for separate high-stakes meetings as the wars in Ukraine and West Asia enter critical phases. The back-to-back talks are expected to focus on the Russia-Ukraine conflict, Iran, regional security and broader diplomatic efforts, with Trump's relationship with the two leaders taking sharply different trajectories in recent months.The meetings come as both leaders arrive to Washington to attend the funeral of late senator Lindsey Graham.According to CNN, Trump will first meet Zelenskyy before holding talks with Netanyahu later in the day. The White House has indicated that the discussions will centre on efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war, the conflict involving Iran, negotiations over Lebanon and the future of the Abraham Accords.Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One on Monday, Trump said Russia's alleged assistance to Iran had little impact on the conflict. He dismissed Zelensky's allegation that Russia was providing Iran with intelligence on US military bases."I don't think they've been doing it, certainly not at a high level," Trump said. "And if they have, it has been very un-impactful." He added that he intended to raise the matter directly with Russian president Vladimir Putin.The remarks came after Zelenskyy on Saturday alleged that Moscow had provided satellite intelligence to Iran that was later used in attacks targeting US military bases and Gulf facilities, while also revealing that Moscow is preparing to receive 30,000 North Korean troops to bolster its forces."The purpose is clear," Zelenskyy had said earlier this month. "None of us in the world should turn a blind eye to one very simple fact: Evil always seeks ways to make things worse and spread further."According to Associated Press, Zelenskyy is expected to follow his White House meeting with visits to Capitol Hill, where he will meet US senators after Graham's funeral at Washington National Cathedral.The visit comes as Republican lawmakers seek to advance Graham's sanctions legislation targeting countries purchasing Russian oil and gas, alongside sanctions against President Vladimir Putin, senior Russian officials, financial institutions and energy projects.Trump and Zelenskyy last met on the sidelines of the Nato summit in Ankara earlier this month, where the US president announced that Washington would grant Ukraine a licence to manufacture Patriot air defence systems.Trump said at the time that he and Zelenskyy had "actually developed a good relationship", adding that Ukraine would be able to produce the systems "pretty quickly".Meanwhile, Netanyahu arrived in Washington for his eighth bilateral meeting with Trump since the US president began his second term.Before departing Israel, Netanyahu made clear that Iran would dominate the discussions."We will discuss all the issues on the agenda, first and foremost, Iran," Netanyahu said in remarks posted on X."Naturally, our goal is to safeguard our security and also to expand the circle of peace around us. I am embarking on this mission with one clear goal - to ensure the security, strength, and future of our dear State of Israel."According to CNN, the leaders are also expected to discuss Lebanon, ongoing regional security concerns and efforts to expand the Abraham Accords.Both Netanyahu and Zelenskyy are expected to attend Graham's funeral in Washington following their White House meetings, underscoring the late senator's longstanding influence on US foreign policy, particularly on Ukraine, Israel and sanctions against Russia.
Article Summary: US president Donald Trump will host Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the White House on Tuesday. The back-to-back meetings are expected to focus on the Russia-Ukraine conflict, Iran, regional security and broader diplomatic efforts. The meetings come as both leaders arrive to Washington to attend the funeral of late senator Lindsey Graham.

Article Title: 'Nobody tells me what we should be selling': Trump rejects Netanyahu's objections to F-35 sale to Turkey
Article Text:
Trump brushes aside Netanyahu's opposition to F-35 sale

US president Donald Trump on Monday brushed aside Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's reported opposition to the possible sale of American F-35 fighter jets to Turkey, asserting that decisions on US arms sales are made solely by Washington.Speaking aboard Air Force One, Trump said no foreign leader influences US defence policy and described Turkey as a "tremendous ally.""Nobody tells me what we should be selling," said the US president. "Turkey has been a tremendous ally for me."Trump had said his administration would soon decide whether to proceed with the sale of F-35 fighter jets to Turkey despite a congressional ban, while also announcing plans to lift sanctions imposed on Ankara over its purchase of the Russian-made S-400 air defence system, CNN reported."We have a better relationship with Turkey, and Turkey has been in many ways much more loyal than other countries that we think would be loyal," Trump said, arguing that Ankara should be allowed to purchase the F-35 fighter jets despite its acquisition of the Russian-made S-400 air defence system.Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has indicated that Ankara believes it is close to finalising a deal with Washington for the purchase of US-made F-35 fighter jets, along with American-made engines for Turkey's indigenous KAAN fighter aircraft.Netanyahu is currently on a visit to Washington and is scheduled to have high-level talks with Trump with regional security and the Iran conflict on agenda.Earlier this month, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu voiced strong opposition to the potential sale of US-made F-35 stealth fighter jets to Turkey, warning that such a move could alter the regional balance of power, CNN reported.Netanyahu said he had personally urged Trump not to approve the sale after Trump indicated he was considering lifting the restrictions imposed during his first term."The sale of America's most advanced fighter aircraft 'doesn't make Turkey a friendly state to the United States,'" Netanyahu told an CNN in an interview."He's not exactly a model ally of the United States," Netanyahu said. "He threatens to destroy my country, the one and only Jewish state," he added.Referring to Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Netanyahu said Ankara is "a regime that's infected with the Muslim Brotherhood, which hates the United States." He warned that supplying F-35 fighter jets to Turkey would have far-reaching consequences for the region.Netanyahu added that he had personally urged Trump not to approve the sale, arguing that doing so would "destroy the power balance in the Middle East."
Article Summary: US president Donald Trump says no foreign leader influences US defence policy. Trump described Turkey as a "tremendous ally" Netanyahu voiced strong opposition to the potential sale of US-made F-35 fighter jets to Turkey. Netanyahu said he had personally urged Trump not to approve the sale.

Article Title: For nearly 100 years, two giant dams trapped this American river. Then one historic decision brought it back to life
Article Text:
How two dams transformed a river in the United States

Why the dams eventually became a problem

Why removing the Elwha dams was far harder than building them

How decades of trapped sediment rushed back to rebuild the river naturally

From river to sea: How the Elwha restoration reshaped an entire coastline

The remarkable return of salmon that revived an entire river ecosystem

Why scientists believe the Elwha River is entering an entirely new ecological era

A turning point for river restoration

For much of the twentieth century, dams were widely viewed as symbols of progress. They generated electricity, supported industry and helped reshape landscapes to meet growing human demand. What received far less attention at the time was the lasting effect these structures had on rivers themselves. Fish migration was interrupted, sediment became trapped behind concrete walls and coastlines gradually lost the natural supply of sand and gravel that rivers had carried for centuries. Along Washington State's Elwha River, those changes remained in place for almost a hundred years. Then a decision was made to reverse them, beginning one of the largest ecological restoration projects ever attempted in the United States.The Elwha River runs for around 45 miles from the Olympic Mountains to the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Before dams appeared on the river, it supported one of the Pacific Northwest's richest salmon systems. The river was also central to the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, whose communities depended on salmon, shellfish and other natural resources for food, livelihoods and cultural traditions.As timber production expanded across the Olympic Peninsula during the early 1900s, demand for electricity increased alongside it.As reported by National Geographic, the first major barrier, the Elwha Dam, entered service in 1914 near the river's lower reaches. A second and taller structure, the Glines Canyon Dam, followed in 1927 farther upstream. Together they supplied electricity that helped drive regional development for decades.The benefits, however, came with lasting environmental consequences. Salmon could no longer reach large stretches of their historic spawning grounds, cutting off access to roughly 75 miles of upstream habitat. Sediment that would naturally have travelled downstream instead accumulated inside the reservoirs, slowly changing the river channel and reducing the material that once replenished nearby beaches and estuaries.By the second half of the twentieth century, the role of the dams had changed. The Olympic Peninsula had become connected to a wider electricity network, leaving the Elwha dams responsible for only a small share of local power generation. At the same time, concern over declining salmon populations continued to grow.Reportedly, legal developments also shifted the discussion. After gaining federal recognition in 1968, the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe became increasingly active in protecting treaty fishing rights. A 1979 United States Supreme Court ruling confirmed that Washington tribes were entitled to half of the state's salmon harvest, strengthening efforts to restore damaged fisheries.During the 1980s, tribal leaders joined environmental organisations in arguing that the ageing dams caused more harm than benefit. Their campaign eventually led Congress to authorise the federal purchase of both dams in 1992 while studies examined whether complete removal could restore the river.Although the decision to remove the dams was made years before demolition began, carrying it out proved far more complicated than constructing them had been. Questions surrounded almost every stage of the project.Engineers needed to decide how to deal with roughly 21 million cubic metres of sediment that had collected behind the dams over nearly a century. Releasing it all at once could overwhelm the river, while leaving it trapped would prevent natural recovery.Rather than using rapid demolition, crews adopted a top-down approach. National Geographic reported, beginning in September 2011, sections of each dam were gradually removed over roughly three years. Lowering the structures in stages allowed sediment to escape progressively instead of arriving downstream in one enormous surge.This careful sequence also protected nearby water supplies. New treatment facilities were built before demolition started, while restoration work included the expansion of fish hatchery facilities managed by the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe.The scale of material released during the first years surprised even many specialists studying the project. Monitoring showed that about 8.2 million tonnes of sediment moved downstream during the first two years alone, several times greater than the river's typical annual sediment transport before removal began.River flows during that period were only slightly above average and major flood events remained relatively modest. Even so, suspended sediment concentrations reached exceptionally high levels at times, while large volumes of gravel and sand also travelled along the riverbed.Scientists identified several distinct periods when sediment movement accelerated. Much of this occurred as former reservoir banks eroded naturally, supplying fresh material into the recovering river channel. At other times, transport slowed because remaining reservoirs temporarily trapped sediment or because seasonal low flows reduced the river's carrying capacity.While these conditions created short-term changes in water clarity, they also restored a process that had been absent for generations.National Geographic reported that the returning sediment did not stop within the river itself. As sand, gravel and finer particles reached the Strait of Juan de Fuca, the coastline around the river mouth started to change.Fresh deposits rebuilt riverbanks, expanded gravel bars and formed around 70 acres of new beach and estuary habitat. These changing landscapes created conditions that favour species including Dungeness crabs, surf smelt, sand lance and various shellfish that rely on shallow coastal environments.Offshore, areas previously dominated by rocky seabed gradually became covered by mud and sand. Although different from the earlier habitat, these new conditions supported another range of marine species, illustrating how river restoration can influence ecosystems extending well beyond freshwater channels.Perhaps the clearest sign of recovery came from the fish that had originally driven much of the restoration effort.Within months of sections of the river reopening, steelhead and coho salmon had moved beyond former dam locations and spawned in tributaries that had been inaccessible for decades. Chinook salmon soon followed, reaching upstream sections that no living fish had occupied for generations.Wildlife responded almost immediately to these returning migrations. American dippers, small river birds that feed in fast-flowing streams, were observed feeding on salmon eggs and young fish soon after spawning resumed. Studies examining nitrogen levels within the birds indicated that nutrients carried inland by salmon were once again entering the surrounding food web.Other species adjusted more gradually. Vegetation established across the drained reservoir beds attracted deer and elk, although local wildlife biologists observed that some elk herds were initially slow to explore these newly available feeding areas despite being nearby.Removing the dams did not erase a century of environmental change overnight. Scientists continue to study how the altered landscape develops as vegetation matures, river channels adjust and wildlife populations respond over longer timescales.The large sediment release itself has permanently reshaped parts of the valley, leaving deposits that are expected to remain visible far into the future. Restoration has therefore created a new river system rather than recreating an exact copy of the one that existed before the twentieth century.Debate has also continued around some management decisions, including hatchery operations designed to support fish recovery. These discussions reflect the wider challenge of balancing ecological restoration with practical conservation measures.The Elwha project has become a reference point for river restoration across the United States. Hundreds of smaller dams have since been removed nationwide, reflecting a broader reassessment of ageing infrastructure whose original purpose has diminished.Large dams remain essential in many parts of the world for electricity generation, water storage and flood management, meaning removal is not always practical or desirable. Yet the Elwha experience demonstrated that where conditions allow, reconnecting a river with its natural flow can revive ecological processes that had been interrupted for generations.Today the river reaches the sea without crossing concrete barriers for the first time in around a century. Salmon again have access to long-blocked spawning habitat, sediment continues to reshape the coastline and the landscape is still adjusting to a transformation that began with the gradual dismantling of two ageing dams.
Article Summary: The Elwha River runs for around 45 miles from the Olympic Mountains to the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Before dams appeared on the river, it supported one of the Pacific Northwest's richest salmon systems. Salmon could no longer reach large stretches of their historic spawning grounds, cutting off access to roughly 75 miles of upstream habitat.

Article Title: Surfside Beach loses $545,598 in sophisticated email scam; Wildcat Construction CEO disputes forensic report, says town ignored red flags
Article Text:
Surfside Beach loses $545,598 in sophisticated email scam; Wildcat Construction CEO disputes forensic report, says town ignored red flags

Fraudsters allegedly posed as contractor

Fake payment request blended into genuine project

Wildcat CEO challenges investigation

Town stands by forensic findings

Payment dispute continues

A payment of $545,598 intended for Wildcat Construction has become the focus of an ongoing fraud investigation in Surfside Beach, South Carolina, after the money was allegedly redirected to a scammer-controlled bank account through a sophisticated email scam.The payment was meant for Wildcat Construction, which was carrying out an underground utility project for the town. According to The Wall Street Journal, the fraud began during what appeared to be a routine email conversation about issuing payment for completed work.Investigators believe someone impersonating a Wildcat Construction employee requested that the town change the payment method from a paper check to an ACH (Automated Clearing House) transfer.The town subsequently sent the money to a bank account in Utah instead of the contractor's legitimate account.The incident is being treated as a Business Email Compromise (BEC) scam, in which cybercriminals use spoofed or lookalike email addresses to impersonate trusted individuals and redirect payments.According to the forensic investigation, fraudulent actors created fake email domains resembling those used by Surfside Beach and Wildcat Construction.Investigators found no evidence that the town's internal computer systems or Microsoft 365 accounts had been breached.Investigators said the fraudulent payment request appeared during an active construction project involving an expected invoice and an existing payment obligation, making it appear legitimate.The forged documentation reportedly included updated bank account information, a callback number and a signature resembling that of Wildcat Construction CEO Alyssa Bowker.The report also found that a town employee attempted to verify the payment instructions by emailing Wildcat Construction's legitimate email address and requesting a callback before processing the transfer.However, investigators said it remains unclear whether the response came from a genuine company representative or from the scammers.Cybersecurity experts say this highlights how modern fraudsters often manipulate existing communication channels, making traditional verification methods less effective.Wildcat Construction CEO Alyssa Bowker has publicly disputed parts of the town's forensic report.According to WMBF, Bowker said Surfside Beach selectively released emails supporting its own narrative while failing to establish whether those messages actually originated from Wildcat's servers.She also claimed the published emails appeared to have had their signatures removed, despite containing Wildcat phone numbers.Bowker further argued that no one from the town verbally confirmed the ACH payment change directly with her or any authorized Wildcat employee.She described verbal confirmation as a standard business safeguard and said several additional warning signs became apparent after the fraud was uncovered.According to The Wall Street Journal, the town's finance director said a staff member called Wildcat's project manager on March 13 before the payment was sent. The project manager referred the caller to Bowker, and a voicemail was left on her mobile phone.Bowker told the newspaper she does not remember receiving the voicemail but acknowledged she may have missed it.Surfside Beach said the purpose of the independent forensic investigation was to determine whether the town's systems had been compromised.Officials said the investigation found no unauthorized access to municipal systems and therefore had no further comment on Bowker's allegations.Mayor Robert Krouse said he believes the payment issue originated on the contractor's side, including the submission of the ACH request.However, the forensic report itself does not conclude that Wildcat Construction was responsible. Instead, it states only that no breach occurred within Surfside Beach's systems.Krouse acknowledged that town officials could have made additional verification calls or rejected the ACH request but described those observations as "20/20 hindsight."He said the town will review its internal procedures and discuss the matter further during an executive session of the town council.Bowker said Wildcat Construction has still not received payment for the project and hopes the dispute can be resolved soon.The town also addressed speculation surrounding the dismissal of finance assistant Brian Gray and business license official Nicole Kindzia, both of whom were fired in June.Officials said the two employees "had absolutely nothing to do with the cybercrime incident." According to the forensic report, the employee who sent the March 13 verification email followed the finance department's established procedures.
Article Summary: Surfside Beach, South Carolina, loses $545,598 in sophisticated email scam. Wildcat Construction CEO disputes forensic report, says town ignored red flags. Town sent money to bank account in Utah instead of contractor's legitimate account. Incident is being treated as a Business Email Compromise (BEC) scam.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Marco Rubio: 'American Dream is a term that is often used but also often misunderstood' and the story of An American Son
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Marco Rubio on what American Dream means to him.

"The American Dream is a term that is often used but also often misunderstood. It isn't really about becoming rich or famous. It is about things much simpler and more fundamental than that It isn't really about becoming rich or famous. It is about things much simpler and more fundamental than that,"

What is American Dream to Marco Rubio?

Long before he became the Secretary of State, Marco Rubio introduced himself as An American Son in his 2012 memoir. At that time, he was a Florida Senator, and also an embodiment of American Dream. Throughout his career which he never planned and his meteoric rise in the current Donald Trump administration, Rubio spoke profoundly about American Dream, about his parents and what these two magic words mean to him.he wrote explaining what American Dream is not."It's a happy home and the ability to live without fear for your safety and that of your family. It's the freedom to worship the way you want. It's the chance to get a good education and a job that allows you to achieve financial security and retire comfortably. And it's about leaving your children better off than yourself," Rubio explained his American Dream."The America my parents came to almost 60 years ago was one where you could find a middle income job even if you didn't have a higher education.That is how they made it to the middle class, working as a bartender and a maid. But they desperately wanted their children to have even more than that. Giving us the chance at a better life was their American Dream," he said."For them, it meant giving us the chance to have what they didn't: a college degree. That is why from a very early age, they would tell me tu tienes que estudiar: "You have to study." And so growing up I never considered not going to college.""My parents did not make enough to save for our education. But I was able to use Pell grants, student loans, work study and summer jobs to pay for a four-year degree and eventually law school."Marco Rubio graduated in 1996 and two years later he ran for the city commissioner of West Miami as he already interened for Ileana Ros-Lehtinen, a Republican who became the first Cuban-American woman elected to the US House of Representatives. Rubio won the election and then his political career was on a fast track. In 1999, ge ran to represent District 111 in Florida. In 2000, he was appoint as Majority Whip and then House Majority Leader in 2002. In 2006, he was elected Speaker of the Florida House, when he was just 35.In 2011, he entered US Senate after winning mid-term election in Florida. He served in the Senate for 14 years before becoming the Secretary of State in 2025.In between, he announced his run for Republican nomination in 2015 but lost primary in Florida.
Article Summary: Marco Rubio: American Dream is not about becoming rich or famous. It's the chance to get a good education and a job that allows you to achieve financial security and retire comfortably. "It's about leaving your children better off than yourself," Rubio said.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Bob Ross: 'The very fact that you're aware of suffering is enough reason to...' and the darkest secret behind human happiness
Article Text:
Robert Norman Ross was an American painter and art instructor

“The very fact that you're aware of suffering is enough reason to be overjoyed that you're alive and can experience it.”

The quiet studio on public television

The Joy of Painting

Simple philosophy in a denim shirt

Living mindfully in a fast world

Standing in front of a wet canvas on television, a soft-spoken painter in a denim shirt painted a stroke of dark brown paint onto a bright landscape. He looked directly into the camera and offered a quiet thought:The sentence sounds strange when you first hear it. Society usually treats pain as a problem—something to fix, hide, or cure with medicine. Yet Bob Ross points to a simple truth about human life. Pain is not a sign that our body or mind is broken. It is proof that we are alive and processing the world. Experiencing heartbreak, grief, or frustration requires an active mind. The pain itself may hurt, but the ability to feel it belongs only to the living.Bob Ross spoke those words during an episode of, the public television show he hosted from 1983 to 1994. Filmed at a small TV station in Muncie, Indiana, US, the show had a low budget, but Ross reached millions of viewers with his gentle voice and simple painting style.The story behind his comment was deeply personal. Ross was grieving the loss of his second wife, Jane, who had died of cancer in 1992. On camera, Ross rarely talked about his personal sad news.He kept his focus on "happy little trees" and soft clouds. In this specific episode, however, he talked about why dark paint is necessary on a canvas to make the light colors show up.He moved naturally from art tips to human emotions. He explained that life follows the same rules as a painting. Without dark moments, the good moments lose their brightness. Ross was not a college professor giving a lecture. He was an art instructor sharing a lesson learned through personal loss, speaking to an audience of late-night viewers, elderly people at home, and tired insomniacs.The logic behind Ross’s words matches ideas from ancient Stoic thinkers and modern philosophers. The ancient teacher Epictetus taught that human beings cannot control outside events, only their own reaction to them. Noticing pain without letting it destroy you is a key part of this ancient mindset.In the mid-twentieth century, psychiatrist Viktor Frankl explained a similar idea in his 1946 book Man’s Search for Meaning. Writing about his survival in Nazi concentration camps, Frankl observed that suffering is an unavoidable part of life, just like death. Without struggle and loss, human life cannot be complete. Frankl argued that when a person cannot change a painful situation, they are forced to change themselves. Recognizing pain becomes the first step toward finding purpose.In terms of psychology, Ross was describing how human senses notice contrast. The brain understands life through comparison. Constant happiness leads to a state where nothing feels special anymore, something psychologists call sensory adaptation. Pain resets our baseline expectations. The sharp sting of loss makes quiet moments of safety and love feel much sweeter.Ross’s point is especially helpful today in a world focused on quick comfort, digital distractions, and instant fixes. Modern culture often treats emotional distress as a personal failure or a technical problem. When human sadness is treated like a bug that needs to be deleted, people lose the ability to deal with basic life struggles.In modern mental health therapy, doctors use a technique called radical acceptance. Created by psychologist Marsha Linehan, this approach teaches people that deep suffering comes from trying to fight or ignore reality. Accepting grief or physical pain as a basic fact of life helps people stay grounded in the present moment instead of panicking about their discomfort.This perspective also changes how people handle failure at work or in life. An athlete healing from an injury or a business owner facing a failed project can view their disappointment as proof that they tried hard. Feeling sad about a loss simply means the goal mattered to you.Ross recorded more than 400 episodes of his show, creating thousands of landscape paintings that were stored in cardboard boxes at his company's office in Herndon, Virginia. He died of lymphoma in 1995 at the age of 52. His paintings remain largely unsold, but the simple mindset he shared next to his easel continues to give people a practical guide for handling all the ups and downs of life.
Article Summary: Bob Ross was an American painter and art instructor. He was grieving the loss of his second wife, Jane, who had died of cancer in 1992. Ross recorded more than 400 episodes of his show, creating thousands of landscape paintings. He died of lymphoma in 1995 at the age of 52.

Article Title: Can ICE or CBP read your deleted messages? Attorney says the answer is 'yes'
Article Text:
Can CBP or ICE access deleted messages on a phone? (AI photo)

What CBP says on checking electronic devices at ports of entry

Many people assume that once a message is deleted, it’s gone forever. But that may not be the reality, attorney Deepak Ahluwalia warned citing a recent case of a client who was stopped at the airport and agents allegedly read deleted messages from the phone. Ahluwalia said the client indicated that he was flying into San Francisco Airport. CBP took his phone and was able to recover permanently deleted messages.Ahluwalia said this incident should not sound completely bizarre given the amount of technology and AI tools the CBP and ICE are using now. "But I found it completely fascinating that despite not being linked to any cloud service, despite having messages permanently deleted, CBP was able to retrieve and read certain messages that ultimately were being used against the entry of the individual," the attorney said."If you’re traveling internationally, it’s important to understand that your electronic devices may be inspected and that digital information may still be accessible, even if you believe it has been deleted," the attorney said.CBP says this happens on rare occasion. "On rare occasions, CBP officers may search a traveler’s mobile phone, computer, camera, or other electronic devices during the inspection process," CBP policy said."These searches have been used to identify and combat terrorist activity, drug smuggling, human smuggling, bulk cash smuggling, human trafficking, intellectual property rights violations and visa fraud, among other violations. They enable the discovery of digital contraband, such as child pornography, illicit transfer of restricted or classified information, or other export-controlled information. Furthermore, border searches of electronic devices are often integral to determining an individual’s intentions upon entry to the United States and thus provide additional information relevant to admissibility of foreign nationals under US immigration laws," it said."The number of travelers crossing the border that experience a border search of their electronic devices is small. In Fiscal Year (FY) 2025, less than 0.01 percent of arriving international travelers encountered by CBP at a port of entry had their electronic devices searched," it said.
Article Summary: Attorney Deepak Ahluwalia says a client was stopped at the airport and agents allegedly read deleted messages from the phone. CBP says this happens on rare occasion. "On rare occasions, CBP officers may search a traveler’s mobile phone, computer, camera, or other electronic devices," CBP policy said.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Taylor Swift's husband Travis Kelce: "If you don't care about the guy next to you, one, you're a terrible…" - why caring about your teammates matters more than individual talent
Article Text:
Travis Kelce

Quote of the day by Travis Kelce

"If you don't care about the guy next to you, one, you're a terrible teammate. Two, you're never gonna win"

What is the meaning behind the quote by Travis Kelce

A real example of Kelce living this out

Why teamwork tends to matter more than raw talent alone

Why genuinely caring about people builds real trust

Why every single role in a team actually matters

Why caring about teammates as people improves performance

Why shared goals bring people together

Other famous quotes by Travis Kelce

"I'm a firm believer that individual accolades are a bit overrated in this game."

"My entire career, you can't say Travis Kelce without Alex Smith. He's been my quarterback, he's been the guy. I owe a lot of my success to him."

"Nobody puts more expectation on me than myself. That's just the heart of the competitor."

"As soon as you get complacent with where you are in a game, that's where you come and then it bites you in the rear. So you just want to make sure that you're keeping that energy high."

Why this quote is relevant today

People love celebrating the star player, the standout entrepreneur, the individual talent who seems to carry a whole team on their back. Travis Kelce , the NFL tight end, pushed back on that picture directly. "If you don't care about the guy next to you, one, you're a terrible teammate," he said. "Two, you're never gonna win." Individual ability clearly matters. What Kelce is pointing at is something that matters just as much and gets talked about far less, whether you actually care about the people working alongside you. It is a simple line, but it says something about winning that gets missed constantly by people focused purely on their own individual numbers."The guy next to you" is not really about friendship here. It stands for respect, trust and a genuine sense of responsibility toward the people you work with. In any team, one person's performance always affects everyone else around them, whether they think about it that way or not.Kelce makes two separate points. First, someone who does not genuinely care about their teammates is failing at one of the most basic parts of actually being on a team. Second, and just as important, that attitude tends to stop the whole group from winning anything meaningful together. Personal excellence on its own was never going to be enough, no matter how talented any single person happens to be.This is not just something Kelce says. In December 2023, his teammate Kadarius Toney committed an offside penalty that wiped out a game-winning touchdown against the Buffalo Bills. Several media figures, including Stephen A. Smith, publicly urged Kelce and quarterback Patrick Mahomes to call Toney out over the mistake. Kelce did the opposite. He defended his teammate directly and pushed back at the media instead of piling on. That is really the quote in action, not just as a line he says, but as something he actually chose to do when the pressure was on to do the opposite.Talent can shift the outcome of a single game, project or assignment, but it rarely guarantees success by itself. A group full of talented people who do not cooperate well often underperforms compared to what they should be capable of. Teams built around genuine communication and trust, on the other hand, regularly produce results that look far better than the sum of their individual parts, because real teamwork lets everyone's strengths actually complement each other instead of competing for attention.Trust builds up once people can see that their teammates actually care whether they succeed or not. A colleague who shares useful knowledge freely, a teammate who offers encouragement after a mistake instead of criticism, a leader who actually notices individual effort, all of these build confidence inside a group. Once that trust exists, people communicate more openly and become far more willing to actually help each other through a hard patch. Kelce's line is really arguing that this kind of care is not just a nice extra. It is a genuine, practical advantage, one that shows up directly in how a team actually performs when things get difficult.Winning teams are almost never the product of one standout individual working alone. In football, championships depend on players, coaches, trainers and support staff all pulling together. The same pattern shows up everywhere else too, in hospitals, in schools, in businesses. Every role genuinely contributes to the final result, and respecting each one, rather than only celebrating the most visible positions, is what actually strengthens the whole group.Treating teammates as actual people rather than simply co-workers tends to build stronger relationships across the board. That kind of empathy encourages patience after a mistake, improves communication under real pressure, and builds loyalty that holds up during difficult stretches. Performance and genuine care were never really separate things. Caring properly about the people around you tends to make everyone perform better, not worse.Strong teams focus on winning together rather than chasing individual recognition. Once people genuinely prioritise the team's goal over their own personal stats or credit, cooperation increases almost automatically, and competition inside the group tends to become healthier rather than more divisive. Success stops being something individuals fight over and starts being something the whole group actually shares.Modern workplaces increasingly depend on collaboration across different skills and backgrounds, which means technical ability on its own is rarely enough anymore. Communication, trust and genuine mutual respect have become just as important as raw skill. Kelce's quote is a reminder that relationships between teammates were never really separate from performance. They are usually the actual reason high-performing teams exist in the first place, on a football field, in an office, or anywhere else people have to rely on each other to get something done.
Article Summary: NFL tight end Travis Kelce: "If you don't care about the guy next to you, one, you're a terrible teammate" Kelce's quote says something about winning that gets missed constantly by people focused purely on their own individual numbers. Kelce is arguing that this kind of care is not a nice extra, but a practical advantage.

Article Title: Netflix executive reveals at company's trust-building retreat he once used ketamine, got fired from his $1.1 million job after return
Article Text:
Netflix executive sues the company for firing him based on what he said at a company outing earlier this year.

A Netflix executive has sued the company after being fired on the basis of what he said at a company retreat earlier this year. New York Post reported that Kevin Baillie said in his lawsuit that the company undertook a 'vulnerability-trust exercise' at a January 2026 retreat at Sendero Ranch, a Northern California property. Baillie has been on the visual effects team for “Pirates of the Caribbean” and the Harry Potter franchise.At that retreat, Baillie shared with his colleagues that he had taken ketamine in 2022 because he was prescribed the treatment after his mother's death.But this admission triggered an investigation against the execurive and he was fired from his $1.1 million a year job and was also denied of severence. The investigator made it look like a recreational drug abuse. In April, Baillie was fired and the company made it clear that his ketamine therapy issue was factored into the termination.Baillie said apart from his ketamine use, the office investigation also checked his drinking and use of vulgar words. He said he had been warned during his performance review that he should "drop one or two less f-bombs but don't stop entirely".The lawsuit said that Baillie drank a Guinness standing on his head at the same retreat as the colleagues were participating in the trust session.He told his colleagues that he could do this trick and that his former father-in-law taught him. The colleagues asked for a demonstration and Baillie showed them the trick.Baille, in his lawsuit, mentioned that the company encouraged alcohol drikining qand Eyeline Syudios CEO Jeff Shapiro himself purchased beer at company outings. In addition to hosting multiple parties, Shapiro also had a personal bar in his office “from which he served alcohol (to Baille) including after a successful meeting with Netflix’s CEO Ted Sarandos,” according to the papers.The NY post report mentioned that Baillie is asking for a jury trial, compensatory damages, lost wages, damages for emotional distress, and punitive damages; and that Netflix and Eyeline have not yet issued any statements.
