is a bigger voice on the world stage if the house is on fire?" former Pakistani ambassador to the United States and the United Kingdom Maleeha Lodhi told the Financial Times."Pakistan needs to fix the cracks within."According to the Financial Times, Field Marshal Asim Munir has sought to address Pakistan's internal instability by transforming the country into what he describes as a "hard state."The newspaper says Munir believes stronger military control is necessary to restore law and order, eliminate militancy, end years of political instability and create conditions for economic recovery.One former US diplomat who dealt extensively with Munir described the army chief's governing style in stark terms."Munir aspires to turn Pakistan into what he calls a 'hard state' and rules Pakistan with a 'massive chip on his shoulder'," the former diplomat told the Financial Times.According to the report, Munir, who became Pakistan's army chief in November 2022, has steadily expanded the military's influence over civilian institutions.The Financial Times says Pakistan's parliament has extended his tenure, granted him greater authority over the armed forces and backed legislation that critics say has weakened judicial independence and curtailed public criticism of the military.The newspaper notes that Munir and his supporters blame years of civilian-led governments for Pakistan's political instability and economic decline.The Financial Times says Pakistan's diplomatic ambitions ultimately depend on economic strength that the country has yet to achieve.According to the World Bank data cited by the newspaper, Pakistan spends substantially less than comparable lower-middle-income countries on health and education, leaving around 25 million children out of school. Nearly 78 per cent of children are unable to read at the expected level by the age of 10, while around 40 per cent suffer from stunted growth.Although the IMF recently praised Pakistan's implementation of its $7 billion bailout programme, the Financial Times says the country's debt burden remains overwhelming.According to Fitch Ratings, interest payments alone are expected to consume around 40 per cent of government revenues by the financial year ending June 2027.The newspaper reports that Pakistan has also sought $10 billion in financial assistance from Washington to strengthen its foreign exchange reserves.Despite official projections of 3.7 per cent economic growth, Pakistan's trade deficit has widened to a four-year high of $39.6 billion, driven by weak exports, rising imports and higher global commodity prices linked to the conflict in the Gulf.Stefan Dercon, an Oxford professor advising Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on economic reforms, warned that policymakers recognise the urgency of the situation."There's a small group of decision makers... that realise if they don't fix this economy, they will fall off the cliff of a deep economic and even political crisis," he told the Financial Times.
Article Summary: Pakistan's foreign policy paradox: Punching above its weight while struggling at home. Mediating between Iran and the United States. Deepening defence ties with Saudi Arabia. Maintaining its strategic partnership with China.Rebuilding relations with Donald Trump's administration. Coordinating closely with Turkey and Egypt on regional security issues.

Article Title: Pakistan: At least 15 killed in suicide attack on Khyber Pakhtunkhwa security check post
Article Text: At least 15 people, including 14 security personnel, were killed after terrorists attacked a joint police check post in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Friday, the military said.According to Pakistan's Inter-Services Public Relations, the attack took place in the Tank district and was carried out by the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).ISPR said the attackers initially attempted to breach the check post's perimeter but were repelled by security forces."The attackers attempted to breach the check post's perimeter, but their attempts were swiftly and decisively foiled by the vigilant and resolute response of security forces," the military's media wing said.The security personnel engaged the militants and killed 15 terrorists during the exchange of fire, it added.The attackers then rammed an explosives-laden vehicle into the perimeter wall of the check post, triggering a powerful blast that caused extensive damage to the facility."Due to blast impact, infrastructure at the check post was seriously damaged; resultantly, 15 brave sons of the soil, including 12 military personnel, two policemen and a government official from the forest department, rendered the ultimate sacrifice and embraced shahadat (martyrdom)," the statement said.The ISPR said a sanitisation operation was underway to track down any remaining militants in the area. It added that Pakistan's security forces would continue counter-terrorism operations under the "Azm-i-Istehkam" campaign."These sacrifices of our brave soldiers further reinforce our unwavering commitment to safeguarding our nation at all costs," the statement added.The attack comes amid a spike in militant violence in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Last week, the ISPR said security forces killed 24 militants in Bannu district and adjoining areas during intelligence-based operations following a recent surge in attacks targeting police and civilians.Earlier in May, at least 15 police personnel were killed in a suicide attack on the Fateh Khel police post in Bannu after militants rammed an explosives-laden vehicle into the facility.
Article Summary: At least 15 people, including 14 security personnel, were killed in the attack. The attack took place in the Tank district and was carried out by the Tehreek-i- Taliban Pakistan. The attackers initially attempted to breach the check post's perimeter but were repelled by security forces.

Article Title: Karachi-bound bus attacked in Balochistan; 3 killed, 5 injured as curfew imposed
Article Text:
In May, Balochistan also witnessed a deadly train bombing targeting security personnel that was claimed by the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA).

Three passengers were killed and five others injured after armed men opened fire on a Karachi-bound passenger bus in Pakistan's restive Balochistan province on Wednesday, prompting authorities to impose an indefinite curfew in the affected area, Dawn reported.According to Dawn, the attack took place in the Garo area of Khud Kocha tehsil in Mastung district. The passenger coach, operated by a private transport company, was travelling from Quetta to Karachi when gunmen positioned on nearby mountains opened indiscriminate fire on the vehicle.Security forces and rescue teams rushed to the scene and shifted the victims to the District Headquarters (DHQ) Hospital in Mastung. The bodies of the three passengers were later handed over to their families after legal formalities, while the injured remained under treatment. Authorities have launched an investigation and are searching for those behind the attack.The violence coincided with a separate explosion that damaged a bridge on the National Highway in the same area. Following the twin incidents, the Balochistan Home Department imposed an indefinite curfew across Khud Kocha sub-tehsil from 9pm on Wednesday.Babar Yousafzai, spokesperson for the Home Department, said the curfew would remain in force until further orders to ensure public safety and maintain law and order. Residents were instructed to remain indoors, with all non-essential movement prohibited. He warned that strict legal action would be taken against anyone violating the curfew and urged people to avoid unnecessary travel.The attack came amid heightened security operations in Balochistan. According to Pakistan's military, security forces killed 10 militants and arrested two female suicide bombers along with their alleged facilitator during intelligence-based operations in Mastung and Surab districts over the past 48 hours.The latest attack adds to a series of militant incidents across Pakistan in recent weeks. Earlier this week, unidentified militants blew up a government middle school in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's Bajaur district. In May, Balochistan also witnessed a deadly train bombing targeting security personnel that was claimed by the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA).
Article Summary: Gunmen opened fire on a Karachi-bound passenger bus in Pakistan's restive Balochistan province on Wednesday. The bus was travelling from Quetta to Karachi when gunmen opened indiscriminate fire on the vehicle. Authorities have launched an investigation and are searching for those behind the attack. The violence coincided with a separate explosion that damaged a bridge on the National Highway in the same area.

Article Title: Borrowed ancestors: Why Pakistan can't claim Panini for its rebranding project
Article Text:
Indus Valley Civilization - Archaeological site of Harappa (Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons)

"Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it."

Ruins are not the same as inheritance

Heritage as reputation management

A civilisation is not a rebrand

— George SantayanaThe land now called Pakistan holds some of the subcontinent's oldest inheritances — the university-town of Takshashila, the brick avenues of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, the birthplace of the grammarian Panini, even a small bronze figure whose cocked hip and bangled arm art historians read as the earliest evidence of dance in South Asia, a gesture some trace forward into the classical grammar later refined into Kathak. For most of its seventy-eight years, the Pakistani state wanted remarkably little to do with any of it.This was not neglect. It was policy. The Two-Nation Theory did not simply carve out a homeland; it required a new ancestry to go with it. Pakistan's intellectual lineage was traced towards Arabia, Persia and Central Asia, and the Vedic, Sanskritic and Indus past lying beneath its own soil was filed away as someone else's prehistory — interesting to archaeologists, irrelevant to the nation. Mohenjo-daro was a curiosity. Takshashila was a footnote. The Dancing Girl was a museum exhibit, not an ancestor.That posture is changing, and the change is official. The Punjab government is currently running a heritage development plan worth close to four billion rupees to restore and rebrand Taxila as a premier tourist destination. Provincial budgets tout the restoration of Harappa and Rohtas Fort alongside Gandhara-circuit tourism drives.Mohenjo-daro is marketed abroad as a UNESCO showpiece. Panini, once an obscure name from a rejected past, is now claimed as a native son. History, apparently, is good for footfall.Consider that Dancing Girl a little longer. She was cast in bronze in Mohenjo-daro, in what is today Sindh, nearly four and a half thousand years ago. A second, cruder casting of the same figure was found beside her. When the subcontinent was partitioned, the finer of the two statuettes went to the National Museum in New Delhi, where she remains the single most reproduced image of the Indus Valley Civilisation. The lesser copy stayed behind, in Karachi. Pakistan inherited the ground she was found on. It did not inherit her.The same split runs through everything else Pakistan is now restoring for tourists. It can excavate a stupa at Taxila, but the unbroken line of Buddhist and Vedic scholarship that once animated that university has no living school inside its borders. It can point to the ruins of Harappa, but Sanskrit is not taught there in gurukulas the way it still is across India. It can rope off Mohenjo-daro for visitors, but the dance grammar its Dancing Girl is said to anticipate is taught today in the gharanas of Jaipur, Lucknow and Varanasi — not in Sindh or Punjab. Geography gave Pakistan the sites. It did not give it the tradition.Why the sudden enthusiasm, then? It is worth asking what else has been happening to Pakistan's standing in the world these past years — the terror-financing scrutiny, the repeated economic bailouts, the image of a state better known for instability than for scholarship. Ancient civilisation is good cover for a troubled present. A country associated with extremism can present itself instead as the cradle of the world's earliest cities and its most rigorous grammarian. Restoring Takshashila photographs well. It is also, transparently, a rebrand.There would be nothing wrong with genuine custodianship. But custodianship is judged by continuity, not by construction budgets. A state that spends on restoring temples and stupas as tourist infrastructure, while showing far less urgency about the living minority communities who are the actual cultural descendants of that civilisation within its own borders, is not practising heritage. It is practising public relations. Ruins do not complain about neglect. Living communities do.None of this is unique to Pakistan — every young nation wants an old civilisation behind it, for the same reason every parvenu wants an ancestral portrait on the wall. But there is a difference between a nation growing into an honest relationship with the past beneath its soil and a nation reaching for that past only once the present has become an embarrassment. The first is scholarship. The second is theatre.Panini's grammar, the ruins of Takshashila, the streets of Mohenjo-daro and the Dancing Girl who stands, unclaimed, in a Delhi museum are not props to be dusted off for a tourism campaign. They belong to a civilisational continuum that long predates Pakistan and that Pakistan's own founding ideology spent decades trying to disown. You cannot renounce an inheritance for seventy years and then present the paperwork the moment the neighbours stop calling.The Panini question, therefore, is not ultimately about Pakistan. It is about how civilizations endure. Nation-states are political arrangements. They emerge, fragment, redraw borders and sometimes disappear altogether. Civilizations operate according to a different logic. They survive because institutions, languages, rituals, philosophies and systems of knowledge are transmitted across generations with remarkable continuity. That continuity cannot be manufactured retrospectively simply because the archaeological site now falls within a different frontier.Panini illustrates this distinction with unusual clarity. His genius did not arise in isolation, any more than Newton's emerged without the European scientific tradition or Confucius without the intellectual world of ancient China. The Ashtadhyayi was the culmination of centuries of Vedic linguistic inquiry, drawing upon earlier traditions of phonetics, etymology and grammatical analysis. It belonged to an ecosystem of scholars, teachers and students extending across the cultural geography of ancient Bharat. His birthplace may today lie inside Pakistan's borders; the intellectual universe that produced him does not.That distinction also explains why heritage cannot be reduced to possession. A ruined monastery may be restored with public funds. A museum may renovate its galleries. Tourism campaigns may attract visitors. Yet the deeper life of a civilization lies not in stone but in continuity. Sanskrit is still spoken, taught and debated. The grammatical tradition Panini codified continues to be studied in universities, monasteries and traditional centres of learning. Classical dance, whose earliest artistic echoes some scholars discern in the Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro, survives through living lineages rather than archaeological exhibits. Civilizations remain alive because their knowledge systems remain alive.There is, in principle, nothing objectionable about Pakistan preserving Panini's birthplace or restoring the monuments of Takshashila and Harappa. Indeed, such efforts should be welcomed. The preservation of humanity's shared heritage is a universal responsibility. The problem begins only when conservation is quietly transformed into ownership, and ownership into civilizational authorship. Geography can preserve monuments; it cannot rewrite the intellectual traditions that created them.Perhaps this explains the growing attraction of ancient heritage within Pakistan's official narrative. Soft power increasingly matters in international politics. Nations seek legitimacy not only through military strength or economic performance but through cultural depth. Ancient civilizations offer prestige, tourism, diplomatic capital and a more attractive international image than perpetual association with conflict or extremism. The impulse is understandable. But prestige cannot rest upon selective memory. One cannot celebrate Panini while remaining intellectually detached from the Vedic and Sanskritic tradition that made Panini possible.History is often generous to those willing to confront it honestly. It is far less forgiving to those who edit it for contemporary convenience. Pakistan is free to acknowledge that some of the world's greatest centres of ancient learning stood on the land it now governs. What it cannot plausibly claim is that the civilization which produced them somehow begins where the modern Pakistani state begins. Civilizations are not inherited through borders. They are inherited through continuity. And continuity cannot be declared by policy, funded through tourism budgets or recovered by rebranding. It has to be lived.
Article Summary: The Punjab government is currently running a heritage development plan worth close to four billion rupees to restore and rebrand Taxila as a premier tourist destination. Restoring Takshashila photographs well. It is also, transparently, a rebrand. Pakistan inherited the ground she was found on. It did not inherit her.

Article Title: Govt school bombed in northwest Pakistan; no casualties reported
Article Text:
Representative image

PESHAWAR: Unknown militants blew up a government school in Pakistan's restive Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, officials said on Tuesday.No casualties were reported in the incident which took place late on Monday, and no group has claimed responsibility for it yet.According to initial reports, unidentified militants planted explosive material at Government Middle School Loi Kharki in the Bajaur district, causing a powerful explosion that extensively damaged the school building.Soon after the incident, law enforcement agencies and other relevant authorities reached the site and launched an investigation.Officials said efforts were underway to determine the nature of the explosion, identify those responsible and ascertain the motive behind the attack.Further investigation is in progress, officials added.According to investigative briefs from Human Rights Watch and the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, militants target educational structures for specific operational reasons.A vast majority of the targeted attacks directly hit girls' institutions to enforce extremist ideological bans against female literacy.
Article Summary: Unknown militants blew up a government school in Pakistan's restive Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. No casualties were reported in the incident which took place late on Monday, and no group has claimed responsibility for it yet. Law enforcement agencies and other relevant authorities reached the site and launched an investigation.

Article Title: 'Failed, inhumane policy': Baloch activist raises alarm over spike in student disappearances in region
Article Text:
According to Baloch, when some of those who later reappear eventually turn to armed violence

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support the involvement of international organizations in addressing human rights issues in Balochistan? Strongly support Do not support 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A recent surge in the alleged enforced disappearances of students and young people in Pakistan's Balochistan province has raised fresh concerns over the treatment of those linked to peaceful political organisations. Human rights activist Sammi Deen Baloch expressed her condemnation of the events and alleged that individuals are being taken from their homes, hostels and educational institutions.In a statement posted on X, Baloch described the development as alarming and a part of a broader pattern of enforced disappearances that has persisted in the restive province."The cycle of enforced disappearances in Balochistan has never truly stopped, but over the past few days in particular, there has been an alarmingly dangerous surge in the enforced disappearances of students," she said in a statement posted on X.The activist alleged that the disappearances were being justified as part of counter-insurgency operations, but argued that the approach had failed to bring peace to the restive province. Instead, she said, decades of such policies had deepened resentment and contributed to a cycle of unrest and violence."Abducting unarmed and innocent students, as well as young people affiliated with peaceful political organizations, from their homes, hostels, and educational institutions and forcibly making them disappear, and then justifying this oppression in the name of counter-insurgency, is a failed and inhumane state policy that has been imposed on Balochistan for decades," Baloch said, "If this approach were truly a means to bring peace, Balochistan would not be drowning today in this quagmire of blood, unrest, and hatred; rather, the reality is that this policy is not fostering peace but giving birth to even more hatred and violence.Baloch further alleged that young people were being held for years without being charged or brought before a court, and subjected to torture, humiliation and other forms of mistreatment. She argued that such treatment could itself fuel anger and a desire for revenge among those affected."When young people are held for years in state torture chambers without any crime or judicial process, subjected to inhuman violence, humiliation, and torment, it is the state itself that nurtures feelings of revenge and hatred against it through its own policies," she said.According to Baloch, when some of those who later reappear eventually turn to armed violence, state propaganda campaigns focus on those who speak out against enforced disappearances rather than examining the circumstances that may have contributed to the radicalisation of young people.She accused authorities of attempting to make the issue of enforced disappearances controversial by blaming peaceful political activists and human rights defenders for allegedly inciting people or recruiting them for armed groups.Baloch argued that the underlying causes of the continuing conflict were instead "illegal actions, state repression, and tyrannical policies", which she said continued to fuel hostility towards the state.She urged the authorities to review what she described as failed, unconstitutional and oppressive policies, and questioned why decades of alleged repression, enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings and collective punishment had failed to establish lasting peace in Balochistan."Instead of offloading the burden of its failed, unconstitutional, and oppressive policies onto the shoulders of the oppressed people and political and human rights activists, the state should ask itself why, despite decades of repression, enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings, and collective punishments, peace could not be established in Balochistan."The Pakistani government has previously rejected allegations of systematic enforced disappearances, maintaining that its security operations are conducted in accordance with the law and are aimed at combating militancy and maintaining public order.
Article Summary: A recent surge in the alleged enforced disappearances of students and young people in Pakistan's Balochistan province has raised fresh concerns over the treatment of those linked to peaceful political organisations. Human rights activist Sammi Deen Baloch expressed her condemnation of the events. She alleged that individuals are being taken from their homes, hostels and educational institutions. According to Baloch, when some of those who later reappear eventually turn to armed violence.

Article Title: HIV outbreak in Pakistan: How deadly safety lapses at Sindh hospital put children at risk
Article Text:
The SHCC's regulatory inspection found that used needles were not being disposed of in sharps bins, hospital staff could not explain disposal of needles (Photo credit: ANI)

At least 78 children have contracted HIV in an outbreak in Pakistan's Karachi linked to serious infection-control and medical waste management failures at a state-run hospital.Findings at the Sindh Employees Social Security Institution (SESSI)-run Valika Hospital in Karachi's SITE area revealed needles manually removed from syringes, inadequate sterilisation safeguards and untrained staff handling contaminated waste.The Sindh Healthcare Commission (SHCC), which conducted a regulatory inspection of the state-run hospital, found that used needles were not being disposed of in sharps bins. That hospital staff could not explain where the removed needles had gone or how they had been disposed of."This raised serious concerns about the hospital's medical waste management practices, as it was unclear where the removed needles had gone or how they had been disposed of," the healthcare commission said.The findings came after a major HIV outbreak at the hospital infected 78 children and led to the screening of more than 10,500 people living in the surrounding area.A further 120 people tested positive for HIV, while six deaths have been reported, according to Dawn.Independent inquiries into the outbreak found widespread failures in infection-prevention practices, including the dangerous reuse of single-use syringes. The findings have raised fresh questions over the safety of medical procedures and the handling of infectious waste at one of Sindh's state-run hospitals.During its inspection, the SHCC found that technical personnel were unable to tell inspectors how contaminated medical waste was being disposed of. The hospital had also failed to provide formal safety training to staff or produce written guidelines for handling medical waste and following infection-control procedures.The condition of the hospital's autoclave, a machine used to sterilise medical equipment, could not be verified. Nursing staff and operation theatre personnel were also absent from their posts during duty hours, making it difficult for inspectors to assess routine infection-control practices."The working condition of the autoclave could not be verified during the visit. Nursing and operation theatre (OT) staffs were also not available during duty time, which was making it difficult to assess routine infection control practices of their duty places," the regulatory body added.The SHCC also found that medical waste was not being segregated and disposed of according to infection prevention and control guidelines. Hospital staff had poor knowledge of safe medical waste handling, while the private contractor responsible for collecting and disposing of the waste had not received proper training."The team found that medical waste was not being segregated and disposed of according to IPC guidelines. Staff showed poor knowledge about safe medical waste handling. The private contractor responsible for collecting and disposing of medical waste had also not received proper training."The hospital's infection-control failures persisted despite the establishment of an Infection Prevention and Control Committee. The commission also cited staff unionisation and a lack of cooperation with safety protocols as factors that had compromised the handling of medical waste.Following independent inquiries, Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah ordered the suspension of 37 officers and officials, including administrators, laboratory personnel and nursing staff.The outbreak has renewed concerns over repeated failures in Pakistan's healthcare system. The country has faced several HIV outbreaks over the past decade, including the 2019 Ratodero outbreak, in which hundreds of children were infected. That investigation also exposed unsafe injection practices, poor sterilisation and weak oversight.The Sindh government has continued screening people in the affected area, promised treatment at public expense and announced a long-term fund for children affected by the outbreak. However, the Valika Hospital findings have raised concerns that similar infection-control failures could exist in other public and private healthcare facilities.
Article Summary: At least 78 children have contracted HIV in an outbreak in Pakistan's Karachi. The outbreak is linked to serious infection-control and medical waste management failures. Inspectors found needles manually removed from syringes, inadequate sterilisation safeguards and untrained staff handling contaminated waste.

Article Title: Pakistan's fifth province? Gilgit-Baltistan assembly passes key resolution amid PoK unrest
Article Text:
Gilgit-Baltistan (AP photo)

Is Pakistan preparing to make Gilgit-Baltistan its fifth province? Amid ongoing unrest in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, the Gilgit-Baltistan assembly has passed a resolution urging Islamabad to grant the region provisional provincial status, a move that could majorly redefine its administrative structure.The Gilgit-Baltistan assembly on Thursday passed a resolution, backed by both ruling and opposition sides, urging Islamabad to grant the region provisional provincial status, according to Dawn.The resolution, moved by lawmaker Jalal Ali Shah, also sought constitutional and political rights for the people of the mountainous region.Gilgit-Baltistan, located in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, currently has a semi-provincial administrative status.Pakistan currently has four provinces -- Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. If Islamabad accepts the proposal, Gilgit-Baltistan would become the country's fifth province under a provisional arrangement.
Article Summary: The Gilgit-Baltistan assembly has passed a resolution urging Islamabad to grant the region provisional provincial status. Pakistan currently has four provinces -- Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. If Islamabad accepts the proposal, Gilgit would become the country's fifth province under a provisional arrangement.

Article Title: 'Take off uniform and contest elections': Pakistani MP's open challenge to its military
Article Text:
Pakistani MP challenges their military ( Image quality improved using AI)

Critique on Baloch and Pashtun region

Critique of military

Petition filed against Fazl over remarks

Pakistani politician and chief of Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl, Maulana Fazlur Rehman, delivered a blistering critique of Pakistan's military and government, accusing them of failing to maintain order in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan while warning that the country's Pashtun regions were "drowning in blood.""The country is falling apart. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa today, there is no government. After the sun sets in the west, until the sun rises in the morning, the police do not step out of their stations. And if the police do not come out of their stations, then the streets will be handed over to armed groups, then the streets and roads will be at the mercy of bandits," Fazl said during a rally Punjab, Pakistan.He directly addressed the military: "I know your authority in my province — you have no government. You are just sitting inside your grand bungalows in the capitals, legs crossed, thinking you are the rulers. At the very least, in my province, you have no government."Fazl said Balochistan had already slipped out of government control and the Pashtun region was now following suit. "In Balochistan, in the Baloch areas, there were rebellions; the entire Baloch region had slipped out of Pakistan's control. Even today, there is no writ of the Pakistan government there.But we were holding back the Baloch region; now the Pashtun region too is drowning in blood."He described the human toll: "In the Pashtun region, within two or three days, we have received more than fifty bodies. All we did in the markets was buy shrouds for our loved ones. All we did was perform funerals for our loved ones."Fazl took aim at military personnel, accusing them of failing to protect citizens despite being paid from public taxes. "Your youth who are becoming martyrs — they have tied the uniform for this very reason, they are taking their salary for this very reason — that they have to fight for the country's security. What favor are you doing me by throwing your blood on me? You are taking your salary from the taxes of my blood and sweat for precisely this. "He added: "I have taken no salary; I will not form any army. You will leave, but you are pushing my homeland toward personal vendettas for generations to come, pushing it toward murder and plunder forever and ever. Explain this politics to someone else; don't try to explain it to us."Fazl challenged the military to enter politics directly. "If you want to do politics, then take off the uniform and come; participate in the elections, and it will become clear what votes people give to those in uniform. It is your prerogative to give government to whomever you want, and to snatch it away from whomever you wish."A petition was filed in a court against Fazl over his remarks, with the petitioner arguing that the speech hurt the sentiments of the general public and caused distress to the families of martyrs. The court sought a reply from the National Counter Terrorism Authority by August 17.Pakistani defence minister Khawaja Asif expressed disappointment, calling Fazl's words "unfair." Pakistan’s planning minister Ahsan Iqbal posted on X: "To describe such an unparalleled sacrifice as merely a compensation for a salary is neither fair, nor in accordance with the demands of ethics, and nor aligned with Islamic teachings."
Article Summary: Pakistani politician Maulana Fazlur Rehman delivered a blistering critique of Pakistan's military and government. He accused them of failing to maintain order in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. He warned that the country's Pashtun regions were "drowning in blood"

Article Title: One killed in communal clash near India-Nepal border, indefinite restrictions imposed
Article Text:
Communal clash leaves one dead

One person was killed and several others, including security personnel, were injured in a communal clash in Nepal's Sunsari district along the India border, prompting authorities to impose indefinite restrictive orders in parts of the district from Monday.According to the District Administration Office in Sunsari, the prohibitory orders came into effect at 7 am on Monday and cover five market areas in the Koshi Province district. The restrictions will remain in force until further notice.The prohibitory orders ban gatherings of more than four people, as well as demonstrations, public meetings and sit-ins in the affected areas.A verbal altercation between members of the two religious groups escalated into violence, prompting security personnel to intervene.The violence broke out on Sunday night in the Kaptangunj area of Devgunj Rural Municipality after members of two religious communities, who were holding separate events, clashed over the use of loudspeakers and the display of religious flags, police said, as cited by PTI.As security forces intervened to restore order, they opened fire, killing 24-year-old Om Prakash Mehta.More than a dozen people, including security personnel, were injured in the clashes, according to police.Authorities said anyone violating the prohibitory orders could face a fine of NPR 500, imprisonment for up to one month, or both.Sunsari district, located in southeastern Nepal, shares a border with the Indian state of Bihar and serves as an important transit and commercial corridor between the two countries.
Article Summary: One person killed in communal clash in Nepal's Sunsari district along the India border. Authorities impose indefinite restrictive orders in parts of the district from Monday. Violence broke out after members of two religious communities clashed over the use of loudspeakers and the display of religious flags.

Article Title: 'Crimes against humanity' complaints filed against Bangladesh ex-president
Article Text:
File photo: Former Bangladesh President Mohammed Shahabuddin (Picture credit: ANI)

DHAKA: Days after Mohammed Shahabuddin resigned as Bangladesh's president, complaints were filed against him with the Bangladesh International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) Sunday, seeking a probe into his role in "crimes against humanity" committed during the '2024 uprising' against Sheikh Hasina government.The charges stem from the same events for which former PM Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia.Shahabuddin - a longtime ally of Hasina who was forced to flee Bangladesh due to the uprising - resigned on Friday, citing health complications."The opposition, including National Citizen Party, has raised the allegations against Shahabuddin. They have every right to do so. But we have found nothing in those allegations that warrants our consideration," home minister Salahuddin Ahmed said.Law minister Mohammad Asaduzzaman, however, said Shahabuddin will be probed for corruption allegations.ICT chief prosecutor Md Aminul Islam said that his office had received two complaints - one from Bangladesh Azad Party and the other from Rastrosonglap Forum."I have not yet gone through the complaints," he said. "Shahabuddin, as the then president, had a role in the killings, torture, and other crimes committed against students and protesters," Rastrosonglap Forum central member secretary Al Nur Mohammad Ayash alleged.
Article Summary: Mohammed Shahabuddin resigned as Bangladesh's president on Friday, citing health complications. Complaints were filed against him Sunday, seeking a probe into his role in "crimes against humanity" The charges stem from the same events for which former PM Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia.

Article Title: Bangladesh orders corruption probe against former president Shahabuddin, a Sheikh Hasina ally
Article Text:
Former Bangladesh President Mohammad Shahbuddin (File photo/PTI)

(With PTI inputs)

Bangladesh law minister Mohammad Asaduzzaman on Sunday announced that former President Mohammad Shahabuddin, who resigned two days ago , will be probed for corruption allegations."The government does not want to do injustice against any person. But the allegations of corruption before his assumption of presidency are being scrutinised thoroughly,” Asaduzzaman told reporters in Chattogram.The minister added that due to "public demand," legal action would be taken following investigations into the allegations against the former president.Shahabuddin, a longtime ally of deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, resigned on Friday citing health complications, two years before the end of his tenure. He had assumed office as president in April 2023, nearly a year before Hasina was ousted in a student-led uprising in August 2024.His resignation came amid speculation that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's government was "uncomfortable" with him. Rahman is the son of former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia, Bangladesh's first woman prime minister and a longtime rival of Sheikh Hasina. Khaleda Zia died in December last year, days after Rahman returned from the UK following 17 years in exile.Meanwhile, Asaduzzaman hinted that Shahabuddin's roles as director of the statutory Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) and later as director of private lender Islami Bank Bangladesh could also come under government scrutiny.Asked whether any overseas travel ban had been imposed on the former president, Asaduzzaman said the matter falls under the jurisdiction of the Home Ministry.On whether Shahabuddin could be arrested, he stated that political parties might raise such demands, but their legal basis would be examined accordingly.Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmed will serve as acting president for 90 days under the Constitution, during which a new president must be elected.Ahmed, who was abroad for medical treatment, returned home early to take charge of the country's highest office.Media reports claimed that Shahabuddin had recently spoken to Sheikh Hasina over the phone, drawing disappointment from the top leadership of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP).However, in an interview with The Daily Star on Thursday, Shahabuddin dismissed the reports as "baseless."
Article Summary: Former President Mohammad Shahabuddin will be probed for corruption allegations. Law minister Mohammad Asaduzzaman said due to "public demand," legal action would be taken. Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmed will serve as acting president for 90 days under the Constitution.

Article Title: Bangladesh President Mohammad Shahabuddin resigns ahead of Sheikh Hasina's planned return, reports of rift with govt
Article Text:
Bangladesh President Mohammad Shahabuddin resigns

Bangladesh President Mohammad Shahabuddin resigned on Friday, nearly two years before the end of his five-year term, Reuters reported citing local media.His resignation comes amid reports that the government was no longer comfortable with his continuation in office because of his perceived ties to former prime minister Sheikh Hasina.Shahabuddin's resignation comes just days after Hasina, who has been living in India since being ousted in the student-led uprising in August 2024, announced that she plans to return to Bangladesh in December and surrender following her conviction by a war crimes tribunal.Under Bangladesh's Constitution, Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad will serve as interim president until a new head of state is elected.According to Reuters, the government had asked him to step down because of his longstanding association with Hasina after she announced plans to return to the country.Shahabuddin, a former ally of Hasina and a nominee of the now-banned Awami League, was elected unopposed in 2023 for a five-year term. He is the last constitutional office-holder from the previous Awami League administration to remain in office following the 2024 uprising that forced Hasina to flee to India.According to Bangladeshi media reports, the government had become unhappy over reports that Shahabuddin had recently attempted to re-establish contact with Hasina. However, senior political leaders said the reasons behind his resignation were 'more complex', particularly after Hasina publicly announced her intention to return.Last November, Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal sentenced Hasina and former home minister Asaduzzaman Khan Kamal to death in absentia for their role in the crackdown on the 2024 student protests, charges she has denied.Shahabuddin, a 1971 Liberation War veteran and former judge, had earlier told Reuters that he intended to step down after the general election, saying he had been sidelined during the tenure of the interim administration that replaced Hasina's government.The resignation comes at a politically sensitive time as the government of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman prepares for Hasina's planned return, which is expected to test the country's political stability after two years of upheaval.
Article Summary: Shahabuddin was elected unopposed in 2023 for a five-year term. He is the last constitutional office-holder from the previous Awami League administration to remain in office. Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad will serve as interim president until a new head of state is elected.

Article Title: Bangladesh President Mohammad Shahabuddin likely to resign soon: Reports
Article Text: Bangladesh President Mohammad Shahabuddin is likely to resign nearly two years before the end of his five-year term, according to political sources and media reports, amid growing speculation that the government is no longer comfortable with his continuation in office.“It is likely that he (Shahabuddin) will resign soon,” a senior leader of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) told PTI without further elaboration.Speculation over Shahabuddin's resignation has intensified over the past two days after several Bangladeshi media outlets reported that the government was considering a change in the presidency. Shahabuddin is the only constitutional office-holder from the previous Awami League administration who has remained in office since the July-August 2024 student-led uprising that toppled then-prime minister Sheikh Hasina 's government. Hasina fled to India on August 5, 2024, where she has remained since.Newspaper Prothom Alo, quoting a high-level government source, reported that the government was unhappy over reports that Shahabuddin had recently attempted to re-establish contact with Hasina.A senior BNP leader also told The Daily Star that a recently reported telephone conversation between Shahabuddin and Hasina was not the sole reason behind the expected resignation. The leader said the issue was "more complex", particularly as Bangladesh's political climate has become more sensitive following Hasina's announcement that she plans to return to the country.Earlier this month, Hasina said she would return to Bangladesh in December. The Bangladesh government said it "welcomed" her decision to return but asserted that she must face justice.On November 17, 2025, Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal (ICT-BD) sentenced Hasina and her former home minister Asaduzzaman Khan Kamal to death in absentia for their superior role in suppressing the protests that are now referred to as the "July Uprising".A 1971 Liberation War veteran and former lower judiciary judge, Shahabuddin assumed office in April 2023 for a five-year term.Under the Bangladesh Constitution, if the president resigns, Parliamentary Speaker Hafizuddin Ahmed will serve as interim president until a new head of state is elected.The ICT-BD was established in 2010 by the Hasina-led government to prosecute collaborators of Pakistani forces during Bangladesh's 1971 Liberation War. Following Hasina's ouster, the Muhammad Yunus-led interim administration amended the tribunal's law to allow it to prosecute leaders and officials of the former Awami League government on charges of crimes against humanity.
Article Summary: Shahabuddin assumed office in April 2023 for a five-year term. He has remained in office since the July-August 2024 uprising that toppled then-prime minister Sheikh Hasina's government. Hasina fled to India on August 5, 2024, and has remained since.

Article Title: Balen ends envoy snub amid protests, to meet India & China ambassadors
Article Text:
Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah. (AFP file photo)

NEW DELHI: Nepal prime minister Balendra Shah is set to break his self-imposed rule of avoiding one-on-one meetings with foreign diplomats by holding separate talks with Indian ambassador Naveen Srivastava and Chinese ambassador Zhang Maoming this week, a diplomatic reset that comes as his govt faces growing street protests and questions over its early policy choices. The two meetings are expected to be held on the same day, an arrangement meant to signal that both India and China remain central to Nepal’s foreign policy.Shah took office on March 27 after riding a Gen Z-driven political wave that promised a break from Nepal’s old political order, but his first weeks in power were marked by an unusual diplomatic posture. He avoided individual meetings with envoys and visiting officials who would ordinarily expect one-on-one access to Nepal’s head of govt, including India’s foreign secretary Vikram Misri, whose Kathmandu visit was postponed after Shah declined to meet him. It was the same story with senior US diplomats, including assistant secretary of state Samir Paul Kapur, who visited Kathmandu in April.Shah’s aides had framed the approach as a "new protocol" under which the PM would not hold one-on-one meetings with foreign officials below foreign minister level, leaving such engagements to foreign ministry channels or collective briefings. Shah also accepted PM Narendra Modi’s invitation to visit India soon after taking office, but that visit has still not taken place.Meanwhile, RSP chairman Rabi Lamichhane received a high-profile welcome in New Delhi in June.Lamichhane’s visit sharpened the contrast. He met Modi, home minister Amit Shah, external affairs minister S Jaishankar, NSA Ajit Doval, Misri and BJP president Nitin Nabin, among others, signalling that New Delhi had opened its top political, diplomatic and security channels to Nepal's ruling party chief.Shah did receive ambassadors and heads of diplomatic missions collectively on April 8. At that meeting, attended by representatives from 17 countries and the United Nations, he spoke of a “balanced and pragmatic foreign policy” and relations based on “trust, mutual respect and shared prosperity”. His govt later presented the format as part of stricter enforcement of Nepal’s "diplomatic code of conduct".Officials familiar with the new development said the decision to begin separate meetings with India and China was deliberate. “It is natural to begin with ambassadors of our two neighbours, India and China, given Nepal’s foreign policy priorities,” an official said, adding that scheduling the meetings on the same day was meant to avoid any perception of preference.The shift comes shortly after Shah’s govt completed 100 days in office, a period in which the street energy that helped bring him to power has begun turning towards his own administration. Protests have broken out over the use of municipal police and bulldozers against Kathmandu’s landless settlements, street vendors and informal workers, with critics saying the city’s poorest residents have borne the sharpest edge of his governance style.Border communities also protested strict enforcement of customs duty on goods worth more than Nepali Rs 100 brought from Indian markets. Anger deepened further after 25-year-old ride-hailing driver Ganesh Nepali set himself ablaze following municipal police action, bringing Gen Z activists, civil-rights voices, informal workers and displaced residents back to the streets.
Article Summary: Nepal's prime minister Balendra Shah is set to break his self-imposed rule of avoiding one-on-one meetings with foreign diplomats. He will hold separate talks with Indian ambassador Naveen Srivastava and Chinese ambassador Zhang Maoming this week.

Article Text:

Why the project matters for India

The big picture

Bhutan has long been the soft, poetic rebuke to a world defined by GDP figures and glitzy 'smart' development models.For decades it has marketed itself — and, more importantly, governed itself — around Gross National Happiness (GNH), a state philosophy that values well‑being, cultural preservation, environmental stewardship, and good governance over raw economic output.Yet beneath the postcard façade, Bhutan confronts a wrenching reality: its youth are leaving in unprecedented numbers.Despite its global branding as the "world’s happiest country", mounting demographic, economic, and social stresses are pushing the nation’s young people to look beyond its Himalayan borders. The country that measures success through happiness faces a paradox — how do you keep a generation content enough to stay when opportunities, mobility, and aspirations pull them outward?To battle the crisis, the country's policymakers and thinkers are rolling out an ambitious concept that is typically Bhutanese: Gelephu Mindfulness City, a high-tech, culturally anchored urban experiment intended to marry economic opportunity with ingrained spiritual and environmental values.This is how a nation built on contentment is trying to stop a brain drain by reinventing what “success” looks like.But before we take a look at the solution, let's decode the crisis facing Bhutan.Bhutan's GNH Index is a unique way the country measures its people's overall well-being instead of just economic growth. Unlike most nations that focus on GDP, Bhutan believes true progress includes mental, social, and environmental health.The GNH Index is built on nine key areas of life: psychological well-being, health, education, time use, cultural diversity, good governance, community vitality, ecological diversity, and living standards. Every few years, the government conducts nationwide surveys asking citizens about these aspects, such as their life satisfaction, sleep, work balance, family ties, and environmental values.People are grouped as deeply happy, extensively happy, narrowly happy, or unhappy, depending on how many indicators they fulfill.The GNH, however, is often misread as proof that the country is the "happiest on earth", but that headline masks a more complicated reality.While GNH reflects Bhutan's unique philosophy of prioritising well-being over GDP, it does not mean citizens are universally content or free from hardship.In global happiness rankings, such as the World Happiness Report, Bhutan typically places around the middle — not at the top.Bhutan’s population is small — about 800,000 — and even modest outflows can distort social and economic balance.Over the last decade youth unemployment, underemployment, and limited higher-education capacity have driven larger cohorts to India, Australia, and beyond for study and work.Bhutan's National Statistics Bureau show increasing temporary and permanent emigration among the age group of 18-35.Bhutanese youth, more connected and aspirational than earlier generations, seek modern career pathways — tech, creative industries, international finance — that the domestic economy struggles to supply.The migration's social costs are multifold.Families lose young wage-earners and future caregivers; rural communities see accelerated aging and labour shortages; the public sector faces recruitment challenges; and the political compact that has long underpinned Bhutan’s social model — citizens invested in a shared cultural and ecological future — comes under strain.External remittances can prop up household incomes short-term but do not build domestic industrial capacity or broaden opportunity inside Bhutan.More significantly, an exodus of young minds weakens cultural renewal — problematic for a nation that takes continuity of identity seriously.Policymakers tried textbook responses to the exodus crisis: expand technical and vocational training, incentivise entrepreneurship, liberalise small-business credit, and pursue FDIs in tourism and light manufacturing. These moves matter, but they collide with structural constraints — geography, a tiny domestic market, limited physical infrastructure, and a deliberate policy preference to limit mass urbanisation and environmental degradation.Bhutan’s constitutional and policy emphasis on preserving culture and environment restricts large-scale industrialisation, while its hydropower-centric growth model offers limited employment multipliers for the modern service and knowledge economy.A new approach needed three elements simultaneously: meaningful job creation aligned with global demand, preservation and modernisation of cultural values, and place-making that makes staying emotionally and socially attractive.Enter Mindfulness City, Bhutan's nascent urban vision. No skyscrapers, highways, massive transport infra and soul-crushing concrete mazes.At its core, Mindfulness City reframes “development” as an integrated proposition: economic opportunity, environmental stewardship, social cohesion, and mental wellbeing — so that modern aspirations are met without sacrificing the emotional and ecological frameworks that define Bhutanese identity.It is less a single project and more a networked policy portfolio: special economic zones for creative technology, campuses for experiential and Himalayan studies, climate-resilient housing anchored by communal public spaces designed for contemplative practice, and tightly controlled tourism nodes that pay locals well and preserve authenticity.Crucially, it anchors economic incentives to GNH-compatible metrics: projects will be evaluated by impact on community well-being, environmental health, and cultural continuity as much as by profit.This balanced approach is designed to answer a key question: can a small nation create a modern urban ecology that satisfies career ambition and cosmopolitan desire, while preserving the psychological and social benefits that defined its national identity?Mindfulness City is not purely hypothetical.Pilots in and around Thimphu and in planned satellite nodes show proof-of-concept: digital nomad visas tied to service provision, a climate data center employing local graduates, and a community-run eco-hospital that blends western medicine with traditional healing practices. Early hires include Bhutanese returnees with engineering and data-science backgrounds working on trans-Himalayan climate modeling—roles that didn’t exist a decade ago in Bhutan.These pilots have produced encouraging metrics: a decline in short-term out-migration from participating districts, higher local retention of graduates in those sectors, and nascent startup formation with Bhutanese founders. Yet the scale is small, and skepticism remains about whether these pilot wins can scale across diverse geographies and social strata.Bhutan’s choices don’t exist in a vacuum. The kingdom sits between India and China, with New Delhi being a dominant security and economic partner.For New Delhi, Bhutan is not just a friendly neighbour; it is a strategic buffer, a hydrological partner, and one of India’s closest and most trusted relationships in the Himalayas. That means any major Bhutanese development project, even one framed as cultural or urban renewal, inevitably carries geopolitical weight.For decades, India has been engaged in Bhutan's infrastructure and education linkages, often in a manner that preserves Thimpu's policy autonomy.This cooperation has extended to Bhutan's ambitious Mindfulness City, which is coming up on the border of Assam's Chirang district.Besides an international airport, the city will also be linked via railway with India.During his trip to Bhutan in November last year, PM Narendra Modi announced the decision to establish an Immigration Check Post at Assam's Hatisar to facilitate easy movement of investors and visitors to Gelephu.India and Bhutan also signed a Memorandum of Understanding on the establishment of two cross-border rail links — Kokrajhar (Assam)–Gelephu (Bhutan) and Banarhat (West Bengal)–Samtse (Bhutan) — to be built at a cost of ₹4,033 crore. The Kokrajhar–Gelephu line will span 69km, while Banarhat–Samtse will cover 20km.The project was virtually inaugurated by PM Modi on March 13 this year.Speaking at a programme in Thimphu marking the 70th birthday of Bhutan's fourth King Jigme Singye Wangchuck, PM Modi said the project would deepen economic and infrastructural cooperation between the two nations.“Along with energy cooperation, our focus is on enhancing connectivity between India and Bhutan because connectivity creates opportunity and opportunity creates prosperity,” he said, adding: "The progress and prosperity of India and Bhutan are closely linked."That is why Mindfulness City matters beyond architecture or branding.If it succeeds, it could slow youth migration, expand domestic opportunity, and reduce the pressure for Bhutanese professionals to seek futures elsewhere.For India, that is important because large-scale outmigration from Bhutan would not just weaken Bhutanese society; it could also increase the pull of India as a labour, education, and transit destination, while making Bhutan more vulnerable to external influence.A stronger Bhutan is easier for India to work with, and far less likely to become a geopolitical opening for China or other outside actors.Bhutan's youth exodus is a wake-up call for any culture that assumes spiritual values alone can anchor modern generations.But the country's challenge is not to stop youth from wanting more. That desire is natural, universal and often healthy.The real task is to make a compelling case that "more" need not mean "elsewhere".Mindfulness City is a plan to make staying an active choice, not a fallback. It is an attempt to prove that modern urban life and spiritual well‑being can coexist — not as a marketing ploy, but as lived reality. It's a philosophical test — can a society scale well-being as an organising principle for economic modernisation?If this works, Bhutan could take its global moral project — happiness measured against wellbeing — and show how to operationalise it where it matters most: in the daily decisions of its people. And the world will get a new template of development where the calculus of migration shifts from "where do I earn the most" to "where do I live my fullest life?".
Article Summary: Bhutan has long marketed itself as the 'world's happiest country' But mounting demographic, economic, and social stresses are pushing the nation’s young people to look beyond its Himalayan borders. How do you keep a generation content enough to stay when opportunities, mobility, and aspirations pull them outward? To battle the crisis, Bhutan is rolling out an ambitious concept that is typically Bhutanese: Gelephu Mindfulness City.
